headline: High: Plandex can write and execute shell commands while the paired prompt-list agent offers no isolation, creating default conflict and cascading-error risk; prompt-injection and compliance risks are lower but nonzero.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: A has no executable surface and is a content-writing prompt repository, while B can read/write files and process stdin/stdout. The only plausible bridge is manual copy-paste or file-based transfer, so injection is possible but not default. Both profiles support that this is a weak interaction path, not a shared channel.
conditions: IF an operator copies A-generated prompt text into B's plan or stdin/stdout, B may follow malicious instructions embedded in that text.
IF A content is stored in a file that B later reads as trusted instructions, prompt injection becomes feasible.
mitigations: Keep A outputs in a separate notes file and never paste them directly into B.
Require a human review step before B executes any plan derived from A content.
Prefix imported A content as untrusted data in B prompts.
Use a read-only staging folder for A artifacts.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between prompt sources and B's instruction parser.

B_data_leakage.rationale: A touches no data classes and has no network egress, while B touches source code and has broad egress plus filesystem access. The pair can leak code or secrets only if sensitive files are placed into B's workspace; A itself does not add a second exfiltration path. This is a shared-workspace risk, but the blast radius is limited by A's empty data profile.
conditions: IF sensitive source code or secrets are present in B's project directory, B can transmit them to external model providers or APIs.
IF A is used to generate prompts that include confidential file contents, those contents can be forwarded into B's context and then egressed.
mitigations: Do not place secrets in B's project directory.
Use a redacted sample repo when testing A-to-B workflows.
Disable or restrict B network access for sensitive projects.
Review B prompts for pasted confidential content before execution.
requires-engineering: enforce workspace-level secret scanning before any B egress.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has no write or execution capabilities, but B can write the filesystem, modify git state, execute shell, and spawn subprocesses. Because B also supports shared state via a Plandex server backend, concurrent instances can collide on mutable resources. The uncertainty is about A's operational role, but the dangerous write side is clearly present in B, so the higher severity is warranted.
conditions: IF two B instances target the same project directory or shared Plandex backend state, writes and git changes can conflict.
IF A-derived instructions cause B to edit the same files repeatedly, B can overwrite prior work without locking.
mitigations: Run only one B instance per project directory.
Pause other B sessions before applying changes.
Commit or snapshot the repo before B writes.
Use separate sandboxes for parallel tasks.
requires-engineering: add file and git locking around shared backend state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: A produces prompt content and B can act on it through review-then-apply or optional auto-apply. That creates a plausible chain where B treats A-derived instructions as authoritative unless a human verifies them. A cannot directly execute actions, so the blast radius is bounded, but the default workflow still allows error propagation.
conditions: IF A-generated text is fed into B as a plan or prompt, B may apply it with insufficient verification.
IF B is run in auto-apply mode, mistakes in A-derived instructions can propagate into filesystem or git changes.
mitigations: Require B to summarize A output before acting on it.
Keep B in review-then-apply mode.
Add a checklist for verifying A-derived claims against source files.
Limit auto-apply to non-production repos.
requires-engineering: add citation/traceability checks from A output to B actions.

E_compliance.rationale: A is an open-source prompt repository with no touched data classes, while B handles source code and model-provider API keys. There is no evidence of regulated data residency mismatch or special certifications, so only a narrow compliance concern remains: B's handling of secrets and code must be kept separate from A's public content. The other agent is not cited for residency because it has no such data flow.
conditions: IF regulated data is introduced into B's workspace, B's external API calls may create a compliance issue.
IF A is repurposed to store internal prompts or secrets, its public open-source distribution becomes a governance problem.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of B's project directory.
Do not store secrets in A's repository.
Review B's API key handling before use.
Separate public prompt assets from private workspaces.
requires-engineering: document data-class boundaries for both tools.
